unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ravensworth Creamery is a private limited company in Country X producing mature cheddar in two maturing rooms. It exports 420,000 kilograms a year to Country W supermarkets, invoiced in dollars at $15 a kilogram, earning $6,300,000, about 60% of its $10,500,000 annual sales revenue. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.50 per euro to $1.25 per euro since March. Currency movements are the single biggest external influence on profits this year.

Managing Director Carla Jimenez must set export prices for next season. Option A is to cut the dollar price to $12 a kilogram, so Country W buyers pay €9.60, to hold orders steady. Option B is to keep the $15 price, accept that Country W orders may fall, and instead win delicatessen listings in Country X. The creamery employs 38 workers and carries $500,000 of bank loans repayable this year.

questions.question_text: Define 'appreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Appreciation is an increase in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys more of a foreign currency than it did before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A rise in the value of one currency
Compared with other currencies / buys more foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the appreciation on Ravensworth Creamery.
questions.model_answer: First, appreciation makes exports more expensive for buyers abroad [k]. At $1.25 per euro, the same $15 kilogram now costs Country W supermarkets €12 instead of €10, so they may baulk at renewing the contract or demand discounts [app]. Second, demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper locally produced cheddar [k]. The 420,000 kg Country W order book, worth $6,300,000 a year, could shrink if supermarkets delist Ravensworth in favour of domestic suppliers [app].

knowledge_max_2: Appreciation makes exports more expensive abroad
Demand for exports may fall as buyers switch to cheaper alternatives
application_max_2: €12 at $1.25 per euro vs €10 at $1.50 per euro for the $15 kilogram
420,000 kg / $6,300,000 Country W order book at risk of delisting

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Ravensworth Creamery might face if it chooses Option A.
questions.model_answer: First, cutting the price shrinks the revenue earned on every kilogram [k]. At $12 instead of $15, Ravensworth forgoes $3 per kilogram across 420,000 kilograms, about $1,260,000 a year of lost revenue [app]. That leaves less cash to repay the $500,000 bank loans this year, raising the risk of refinancing at worse terms or missing repayments [an]. Second, a sharp price cut can provoke rival suppliers into cutting prices too [k]. Country W rivals may match the €9.60 shelf price to defend their own listings [app]. Margins then stay permanently lower across the category, so Ravensworth struggles to fund the two maturing rooms and its 38 workers even after winning orders back [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting price reduces revenue earned per unit
Lower prices can trigger a price war with rival suppliers
application_max_2: $3 per kilogram x 420,000 kg is about $1,260,000 of lost revenue
Reference to €9.60 shelf price being matched by Country W rivals
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower price to lower revenue to difficulty repaying $500,000 bank loans
Chain from price war to permanently lower margins and funding pressure on maturing rooms and staff

questions.question_text: Do you think Ravensworth Creamery should cut the export price to $12 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts the price by 20% to $12 a kilogram [k]. At the new rate Country W buyers pay €9.60, below the €10 they paid before the appreciation, so the 420,000 kg order book worth $6,300,000 is far more likely to hold [app]. Keeping the Country W contract fills both maturing rooms, protects the jobs of 38 workers, and avoids the slow, risky push into delicatessens in Country X where volumes are much smaller [an]. However, Option B holds the $15 price [k]. Refusing to discount avoids forgoing $1,260,000 a year, keeping cash flow stronger for the $500,000 bank loan repayments, and it bets on higher-margin delicatessen listings instead [app]. The danger is that Country W supermarkets, now facing €12 per kilogram, delist Ravensworth altogether and leave it with idle capacity and falling sales [an]. Overall, I think Ravensworth should choose Option A [eval]. The appreciation was driven by currency markets, not by anything Ravensworth failed to do, so protecting volume and shelf space in Country W matters more than squeezing the margin per kilogram, and the price can be reviewed if the dollar weakens next season [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: cut the dollar price to $12 (€9.60) to defend export volume
Option B: hold the $15 price and pursue Country X delicatessen listings
application_max_2: €9.60 at $1.25 per euro vs €12 at the held $15 price / €10 before the appreciation
Reference to 420,000 kg / $6,300,000 of Country W sales / $1,260,000 / $500,000 loans
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to retained Country W volume and filled maturing rooms
Chain from holding the price to preserved margin but risk of delisting and idle capacity
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and notes the exchange-rate cause of the problem

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Netherfield Glassworks is a private limited company in Country X producing toughened glass panels for office towers. It imports 500 tonnes of glass blanks a year from Country W, invoiced in euros at €4,000 a tonne. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro, so the $2,600,000 annual bill is now $3,120,000, an extra $520,000 a year.

Finance Director Priya Nair must decide how to cover the increase. Option A is to absorb it from the $380,000 retained-profit reserve. Option B is to raise prices by 12% across its $4,400,000 annual sales, adding $528,000. The firm employs 26 glass technicians and three big customers hold fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000. The tempering oven due in June is already paid for.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of 500 tonnes of glass blanks before and after the rate change.

knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation before the change: $2,600,000
Correct calculation after the change: $3,120,000

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Netherfield Glassworks.
questions.model_answer: First, imports become more expensive when the currency weakens [k]. The annual glass blank bill rises from $2,600,000 to $3,120,000, an extra $520,000 a year for exactly the same 500 tonnes of inputs [app]. Second, higher input costs squeeze the profit margin [k]. The $380,000 retained-profit reserve is not enough to absorb a $520,000 rise, so Netherfield must cut costs, raise prices or eat into the reserve [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
Higher costs squeeze profit margins
application_max_2: Import bill rises from $2,600,000 to $3,120,000 (extra $520,000)
$380,000 reserve is insufficient to cover the extra $520,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of choosing Option B, to raise prices by 12%.
questions.model_answer: First, customers may resist a double-digit price rise and switch to cheaper rivals [k]. The three big customers' contracts are fixed-price worth $1,900,000, so the 12% rise cannot touch them; the full $528,000 must come from smaller and new customers, who are the most price-sensitive [app]. If they defer or cancel orders, sales fall below $4,400,000 and the expected $528,000 gain shrinks fast [an]. Second, raising prices may trigger wider price competition in the office-tower market [k]. Rival glassworks may hold prices to grab Netherfield's share, leaving it with fewer orders to spread fixed costs across [app]. Falling volumes raise unit costs, cutting profit at a time when the $380,000 reserve is already stretched by the $520,000 import rise [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing customers to cheaper rivals
Price rises can trigger competitive price cuts / lost volume
application_max_2: Fixed-price contracts worth $1,900,000 cannot be repriced, so the rise falls on smaller customers
Reference to $528,000 expected gain vs $4,400,000 sales and the $380,000 reserve
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to lost orders to sales below $4,400,000 and a shrinking gain
Chain from competition on price to lower volume to higher unit costs and lower profit

questions.question_text: Do you think Netherfield Glassworks should raise prices by 12% (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B raises prices by 12% across $4,400,000 of annual sales, adding $528,000 a year [k]. That more than covers the extra $520,000 import bill and leaves $8,000 spare, restoring the $380,000 reserve for genuine emergencies such as a machine breakdown [app]. Holding real prices up protects the margin needed to keep the 26 technicians busy and avoids eating into reserves that took years to build [an]. However, Option A absorbs the $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve [k]. This keeps Netherfield fully competitive on price and protects relationships with the three fixed-price customers while their contracts run, which may win follow-on work after next summer [app]. The danger is that the reserve is wiped out entirely and still leaves $140,000 unfunded, so the firm enters winter with no cushion if the dollar weakens further or if repairs arise [an]. Overall, I think Netherfield should choose Option B [eval], because absorbing a $520,000 rise it cannot afford is riskier than the possible loss of price-sensitive orders; the firm should apply the rise to new work first and soften it if order volumes fall sharply [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B: 12% price rise adding $528,000 a year
Option A: absorb the extra $520,000 from the $380,000 reserve
application_max_2: $528,000 gain vs $520,000 extra cost / $8,000 surplus
$380,000 reserve cannot cover $520,000 (shortfall $140,000) / $1,900,000 fixed contracts
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to restored reserve and financial safety
Chain from absorbing the cost to exhausted reserve and no cushion for further depreciation
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and notes linking the rise to new work first

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Whinmoor Wool Exports is a partnership in Country X combing and dyeing wool tops on two lines in a converted mill. It sells 70% of its 120,000 kg annual output to garment factories in Country W, invoiced in euros at €18 a kilogram — 84,000 kg worth €1,512,000. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.25 per euro to $1.50 per euro, lifting dollar receipts from $1,890,000 to $2,268,000.

Partners Dana Whitmore and Ruth Iyer must decide how to respond. Option A is to chase 25 new Country W accounts while wool tops are cheap abroad. Option B is to sign a three-year domestic supply contract with knitwear mills in Country X at a fixed dollar price. The partnership employs 19 dyers and expects sheep prices to climb 10% next year.

questions.question_text: Define 'depreciation'.
questions.model_answer: Depreciation is a fall in the value of one currency against other currencies, so the currency buys less of a foreign currency than it did before [2].

knowledge_max_2: A fall in the value of one currency
Compared with other currencies / buys less foreign currency than before

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the weaker currency for Whinmoor Wool Exports.
questions.model_answer: First, a weaker currency means each euro of Country W sales converts into more dollars [k]. The 84,000 kg exported at €18 per kilogram bring in €1,512,000, worth $2,268,000 now instead of $1,890,000 at the old rate — an extra $378,000 for no extra output [app]. Second, a weaker currency makes Whinmoor's wool tops cheaper for overseas buyers [k]. Country W garment factories can now buy the same combed, dyed yarn for fewer euros, which should help Whinmoor win the 25 new accounts it is chasing [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation raises the local currency value of foreign earnings
A depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad / more competitive
application_max_2: Reference to 70% of output exported to Country W / chasing 25 new accounts

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to chase 25 new Country W accounts.
questions.model_answer: First, adding new export accounts raises output volumes and revenue [k]. Selling into 25 additional Country W factories could lift the current 84,000 kg export run-rate well beyond 70% of the 120,000 kg annual output [app]. Higher volume keeps both lines near capacity, spreading fixed mill costs over more kilograms and lifting profit per kilogram [an]. Second, the weaker currency gives Whinmoor room to win share without cutting its €18 price [k]. Country W buyers see the same yarn effectively cheaper to their shareholders at $1.50 per euro, even while Whinmoor still receives $27 a kilogram [app]. Winning the accounts now locks in revenue before sheep prices climb 10% next year, protecting margins while the currency advantage lasts [an].

knowledge_max_2: New accounts raise export sales volume and revenue
A weaker currency allows winning share without cutting the foreign price
application_max_2: Reference to 84,000 kg current exports / 70% of 120,000 kg output
Reference to €18 price / $1.50 per euro / 25 new Country W accounts
analysis_max_2: Chain from more accounts to fuller capacity to lower unit costs and higher profit
Chain from currency advantage to locked-in revenue before sheep prices climb 10%

questions.question_text: Do you think Whinmoor Wool Exports should chase 25 new Country W accounts (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A commits the partnership to chasing 25 new Country W accounts while the currency favours exporters [k]. At $1.50 per euro, euro invoices at €18 a kilogram bring $27 a kilogram, so extra orders add directly to the $2,268,000 already expected, and spreading output across more customers reduces reliance on the existing 84,000 kg order book [app]. If the two lines run closer to capacity, fixed mill costs spread further, although chasing accounts costs sales time and extra working capital for dyeing and shipping the additional tops [an]. However, Option B signs a three-year domestic supply contract with Country X knitwear mills at a fixed dollar price [k]. It gives the partnership certainty over volume and price, insulating it from a rebound in the dollar and from the expected 10% rise in sheep prices, making cash flow easy to plan for its 19 dyers [app]. The risk is that it locks in fixed dollar prices just as the currency advantage is paying out, and domestic mills may demand keen prices because they know exporters need volume, capping margins for three years [an]. Overall, I think Whinmoor should choose Option A [eval], because the depreciation window is temporary and export demand is already proven by 70% of output going to Country W, so capturing new accounts now builds lasting positions; the domestic contract remains a sensible fallback if sheep costs rise 10% as feared [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: chase 25 new Country W accounts while the currency is favourable
Option B: three-year domestic contract at a fixed dollar price
application_max_2: Reference to $27 per kg at $1.50 per euro vs €18 price and the $2,268,000 export revenue
Reference to 84,000 kg / 70% of output / 19 dyers / expected 10% sheep price rise
analysis_max_2: Chain from new accounts to fuller capacity to better spread of fixed costs and profits
Chain from fixed domestic contract to cost certainty but capped margins and lost currency upside
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and the expected sheep price rise

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Quillbeck Leather Co is a private limited company in Country X cutting and stitching leather shoulder bags for high-street shops. It imports 25,000 square metres of calfskin a year from Country W at €60 a square metre, a bill of $2,250,000 at $1.50 per euro. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.50 per euro to $1.20 per euro, cutting the bill to $1,800,000, a saving of $450,000.

Owner Beatriz Quintero must decide what to do with the saving. Option A is to cut retail prices by 5% across its $3,600,000 of annual shop sales, giving up $180,000 to win market share. Option B is to hold prices and bank the extra margin. The company employs 22 cutters and sewers and sells through 60 shops in Country X.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a stronger currency on consumers.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods and foreign products become cheaper, so consumers can buy more for their money [1]. Holidays and goods bought abroad cost less in local currency, stretching consumers' purchasing power further [1].

knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper for consumers
Consumer purchasing power rises / foreign travel and imports cost less

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Quillbeck Leather Co.
questions.model_answer: First, imports become cheaper for the business [k]. The 25,000 square metres of calfskin now cost $1,800,000 a year instead of $2,250,000, saving $450,000 on its single biggest input [app]. Second, lower input costs improve profit margins without raising prices [k]. Even if only part of the saving is banked, margins on bags sold through its 60 shops improve, leaving more profit available for wages, materials and future investment [app].

knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency makes imports cheaper for the business
Lower import costs improve profit margins
application_max_2: Calfskin bill falls from $2,250,000 to $1,800,000 (saving $450,000)
Reference to sales through 60 shops / 25,000 square metres of calfskin

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of choosing Option A, to cut retail prices by 5%.
questions.model_answer: First, lower shelf prices attract price-sensitive shoppers and lift sales volume [k]. Giving up $180,000 across $3,600,000 of annual shop sales is affordable because the import saving is $450,000, leaving $270,000 of the saving to bank [app]. Extra footfall should raise sales of bags and accessories together, lifting total revenue beyond the $180,000 given up [an]. Second, passing on part of the saving builds goodwill and loyalty among regular customers [k]. Shoppers at the 60 shops see leather goods become more affordable, which encourages repeat visits and word-of-mouth recommendations [app]. Stronger loyalty consolidates Quillbeck's position before rivals match the cut, making future price rises or new range launches easier to accept [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower prices attract customers and increase sales volume
Passing on savings builds goodwill and customer loyalty
application_max_2: $180,000 cost of the 5% cut is affordable from the $450,000 saving (leaving $270,000)
Reference to $3,600,000 shop sales / 60 shops
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower prices to higher footfall to more than offsetting the $180,000 given up
Chain from passed-on savings to loyalty to defending share against rival matching

questions.question_text: Do you think Quillbeck Leather Co should cut retail prices by 5% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts retail prices by 5% across its $3,600,000 of annual shop sales, giving up $180,000 of revenue [k]. The import saving is larger at $450,000, so after funding the cut Quillbeck still retains $270,000 of extra margin, and cheaper bags can win new shoppers across its 60 Country X shops [app]. Attracting price-sensitive customers now builds loyalty and shelf presence ahead of peak seasons, and higher footfall may lift accessory sales as well as bags [an]. However, Option B holds prices and banks the full $450,000 margin [k]. That strengthens retained profit for investment, cushions the business if the dollar slips back against the euro, and avoids the risk that the 5% cut fails to lift volumes — $180,000 is a real cost even if shoppers barely notice [app]. Holding prices also protects the existing margin if wages or transport costs rise later, though rivals may undercut it if they pass on their own savings [an]. Overall, I think Quillbeck should choose Option A [eval], because a 5% cut is affordable from a $450,000 saving and the loyalty and share gains in its home market are worth more than banking the margin now; it should review the cut after two months and restore prices if footfall does not rise [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 5% price cut costing $180,000 to win market share
Option B: hold prices and bank the $450,000 margin saving
application_max_2: $180,000 of the $450,000 saving returned to shoppers, leaving $270,000
Reference to $3,600,000 shop sales / 60 shops / $1,800,000 calfskin bill
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to higher footfall and loyalty to long-term share gains
Chain from holding prices to banked margin but loss of competitive goodwill if rivals pass on savings
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the cut

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Holmfirth Surgical Instruments is a private limited company in Country X producing bone drills for export to hospitals in Country W. It sells 320 sets a year at €2,400 each, about €768,000. The dollar-euro rate swung between $1.20 and $1.50 over the past 12 months, so dollar receipts move between $921,600 and $1,152,000, a gap of $230,400.

Managing Director Yusuf Rahman must set the price list for next year's contracts. Option A is to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set, shifting currency risk to buyers. Option B is to invoice in euros at €2,400 a set and carry the dollar uncertainty. The firm employs 17 machinists and banks through a Country X clearing bank. Each 0.10 move in the rate shifts annual cash by about $76,800.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by 'exchange-rate fluctuation'.
questions.model_answer: Exchange-rate fluctuation is when the value of one currency against another rises and falls over time rather than staying fixed, so the price of foreign currencies changes frequently [2].

knowledge_max_2: The value of one currency against another changes over time
Rates are not fixed / they move up and down frequently

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the fluctuation creates for Holmfirth Surgical Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, export earnings in dollars become unpredictable [k]. The 320 sets sold each year at €2,400, worth €768,000, can yield $921,600 at the low point of the range or $1,152,000 at the high point, a swing of $230,400 on identical orders [app]. Second, the firm finds budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult [k]. It cannot fix monthly dollar inflows, making it hard to schedule wages for 17 machinists or to plan equipment purchases with confidence [app].

knowledge_max_2: Fluctuations make foreign-currency earnings unpredictable
Fluctuations make budgeting and cash-flow planning difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600 at the low point and $1,152,000 at the high point
Reference to the $230,400 gap / 320 sets / €768,000 a year

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to invoice in Country X dollars at $3,000 a set.
questions.model_answer: First, dollar invoicing removes the exchange-rate risk from Holmfirth entirely [k]. At $3,000 a set the firm knows it will receive about $960,000 a year for 320 sets, whatever happens between $1.20 and $1.50 [app]. Predictable receipts let it budget wages, materials and the clearing-bank account without guessing each month's conversion, cutting financial stress and borrowing costs [an]. Second, invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and management reports [k]. All 320 export invoices are written and collected in dollars, so no conversion work or foreign-currency bank charges apply to each deal [app]. Management can compare monthly performance directly against equivalent euro figures, improving control and the speed of decision-making [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the home currency removes exchange-rate risk for the seller
Invoicing in the home currency simplifies bookkeeping and administration
application_max_2: $3,000 x 320 sets is about $960,000 a year regardless of the rate between $1.20 and $1.50
Reference to 320 sets a year / Country X clearing bank
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed dollar receipts to reliable budgeting to lower stress and borrowing costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to simpler administration to faster, better-informed decisions

questions.question_text: Do you think Holmfirth Surgical Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in dollars at $3,000 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A invoices in Country X dollars at $3,000 per set, fixing annual revenue at about $960,000 for 320 sets [k]. It removes the $230,400 swing between the low and high points of the dollar-euro range, making wages for 17 machinists and loan repayments easy to plan, and it spares the firm conversion fees and extra paperwork [app]. The trade-off is that Country W hospitals face a euro price that moves with the rate — at $1.50 the price is €2,000 and at $1.20 it is €2,500 — so buyers may push back or compare rival quotes, which could cost Holmfirth orders [an]. However, Option B invoices in euros at €2,400 per set [k]. Buyers see a stable euro price, which they prefer, and it may help Holmfirth win and keep hospital contracts against rival suppliers whose quotes also move with the rate [app]. The cost is that Holmfirth carries the full currency risk itself, so a year of adverse rates could cost $230,400 of margin, out of earnings of between $921,600 and $1,152,000 [an]. Overall, I think Holmfirth should choose Option A [eval], because the swing is worth about $230,400 a year — too large to gamble on hospital loyalty, and the firm can discount individual deals if a buyer complains, whereas it cannot recover euro invoices already written; it should review the $3,000 price each quarter as the rate moves [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: dollar invoicing at $3,000 fixes revenue at about $960,000
Option B: euro invoicing at €2,400 gives buyers price stability but Holmfirth carries the risk
application_max_2: Reference to $921,600–$1,152,000 range and the $230,400 gap
Reference to 320 sets / €2,400 / $3,000 / 17 machinists / Country W hospitals
analysis_max_2: Chain from dollar invoicing to revenue certainty to easier wages and loan planning
Chain from euro invoicing to buyer price stability but $230,400 of currency risk for Holmfirth
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes quarterly price review

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Brayford Marine Engines is a private limited company in Country X importing outboard motors from Country W, invoiced in euros at €3,100 each. It sells 240 motors a year at an average retail price of $5,400, earning $1,296,000. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.25 per euro to $1.50 per euro, so the import bill rose from $930,000 to $1,116,000, an extra $186,000 a year.

Managing Director Mark Davison must set the spring price list. Option A is to raise retail prices by 20% to $6,480, adding $259,200 a year. Option B is to hold $5,400 and absorb the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve. The company employs 9 fitters and a workshop service manager. Crews pay cash, so price rises are felt immediately at the dock.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar cost of 240 outboard motors at €3,100 each before and after the rate change.

knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation before the change: $930,000
Correct calculation after the change: $1,116,000

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Brayford Marine Engines.
questions.model_answer: First, imported motors become more expensive in local currency [k]. The 240 motors a year rise from a $930,000 to a $1,116,000 import bill, an extra $186,000 a year for the same stock [app]. Second, margins are squeezed if prices are held at $5,400 [k]. Holding price absorbs $186,000 of the $260,000 profit reserve, leaving just $74,000 of cover for the whole year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
Holding prices squeezes profit margins / cash reserves
application_max_2: Import bill rises from $930,000 to $1,116,000 (extra $186,000)
$260,000 reserve left with only about $74,000 after absorbing $186,000

questions.question_text: Explain two problems of choosing Option A, to raise prices by 20% to $6,480.
questions.model_answer: First, a 20% price rise may drive fishing crews to rival importers or the used-motor market [k]. Moving from $5,400 to $6,480 adds $1,080 to each motor, and crews working on tight margins may simply delay replacing engines [app]. Every ten motors lost cuts $64,800 of revenue, so losing more than forty motors a year would wipe out the $259,200 gain from the rise [an]. Second, the rise may trigger retaliatory discounting across the small-engine market [k]. Brayford's nine fitters could be left with idle workshop hours if demand falls away [app]. Idle capacity spreads fixed workshop costs over fewer units, pushing up unit costs and eroding the very margin the price rise was meant to protect [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices risk losing price-sensitive customers to rivals
Price rises can trigger competitor discounting and lower volume
application_max_2: Reference to $1,080 increase per motor / 240 motors a year / $259,200 expected gain
Reference to fishing crews being price-sensitive and 9 fitters facing idle hours
analysis_max_2: Chain from lost sales to revenue falling to the point that $259,200 gain is erased
Chain from lower volume to fixed costs spread over fewer units to higher unit costs

questions.question_text: Do you think Brayford Marine Engines should raise retail prices by 20% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A raises the retail price by 20% to $6,480, adding $1,080 per motor and about $259,200 a year at 240 motors [k]. That more than covers the extra $186,000 import cost and would rebuild the profit reserve, a strong position if the dollar falls further [app]. The margin of safety is also comfortable: Brayford can lose about forty motor sales a year, roughly one sixth of volume, before the rise loses its benefit [an]. However, Option B holds the $5,400 price and absorbs the $186,000 rise from the $260,000 profit reserve [k]. Holding prices protects goodwill with fishing crews and ferry operators who buy on reputation and aftercare, keeping the order book and workshop utilisation stable [app]. The risk is that the reserve falls to about $74,000, leaving almost no cover if the rate weakens again or if warranty claims arrive, which could force an emergency loan at painful interest [an]. Overall, I think Brayford should choose Option A [eval], because the price rise stays well ahead of the reserve cushion even after realistic customer losses, and absorbing a permanent $186,000 cost into a $74,000 reserve would be reckless; it should monitor weekly orders and soften the rise if sales collapse [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 20% rise to $6,480, about $259,200 extra a year
Option B: hold $5,400 and absorb $186,000 from the $260,000 reserve
application_max_2: $259,200 gain vs $186,000 extra cost / margin of safety of about forty motors
Reference to $260,000 reserve falling to about $74,000 under Option B / 240 motors / $1,296,000 sales
analysis_max_2: Chain from price rise to covered import bill to rebuilt reserve and resilience
Chain from holding price to exhausted reserve to risk of emergency borrowing
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring weekly orders

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ossett Digital Stores is a regional electronics retailer in Country X with 6 shops across the midlands. It imports 20,000 tablets a year from Country W at €150 each, invoiced in euros. The Country X dollar has appreciated from $1.60 per euro to $1.28 per euro, so the cost of each tablet fell from $240 to $192, saving $48 each.

Owner Nadia Hussain must decide the autumn promotion. Option A is to cut shelf prices by 8% across $6,000,000 of tablet sales, giving up $480,000 to advertise record value. Option B is to hold prices and use the saving to fund a 7th shop in the northern suburbs. The chain employs 34 staff, made $410,000 profit last year, and tablets are its highest-margin line.

questions.question_text: State two ways consumers benefit when their country's currency appreciates.
questions.model_answer: Imported goods and foreign products become cheaper, so consumers get more for their money [1]. Holidays and purchases abroad cost less in local currency, stretching consumers' budgets further [1].

knowledge_max_2: Imported goods become cheaper for consumers
Purchasing power rises / foreign spending costs less in local currency

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits of the appreciation for Ossett Digital Stores.
questions.model_answer: First, the imported tablets it sells cost less to buy in [k]. Each of the 20,000 tablets falls from $240 to $192, saving $48 each — about $960,000 across the year's purchases [app]. Second, Ossett's margins improve if it holds prices while costs fall [k]. The $48 saving on every unit drops straight to profit on $6,000,000 of tablet sales, comfortably lifting profit beyond the $410,000 made last year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A stronger currency makes imports cheaper to buy
Lower import costs improve profit margins
application_max_2: Tablet cost falls from $240 to $192 (saving $48 each)
Reference to $6,000,000 of tablet sales / $410,000 profit last year / 20,000 tablets

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to cut shelf prices by 8%.
questions.model_answer: First, lower prices attract value-hungry shoppers away from rivals [k]. Cutting 8% off $6,000,000 of sales returns $480,000 to customers as savings, a strong headline claim for in-store and local advertising [app]. If footfall and basket sizes rise even modestly, tablet and accessory sales together could far outweigh the $480,000 given up [an]. Second, passing on part of the saving builds goodwill and defends market share [k]. Consumers benefit directly from cheaper tablets, strengthening Ossett's value image across the midlands [app]. A reputation for passing on savings makes future promotions more trusted, supporting volume ahead of the 7th shop and spreading fixed costs over more sales [an].

knowledge_max_2: Lower prices attract customers and grow sales volume
Passing on savings builds goodwill and loyalty
application_max_2: Reference to 8% off $6,000,000 = $480,000 returned to shoppers
Reference to the $48 per-tablet import saving / 6 shops across the midlands
analysis_max_2: Chain from lower prices to higher footfall to sales outweighing the $480,000 given up
Chain from passed-on savings to goodwill to defending share ahead of the 7th shop

questions.question_text: Do you think Ossett Digital Stores should cut shelf prices by 8% (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A cuts shelf prices by 8% across $6,000,000 of tablet sales, giving up $480,000 of revenue [k]. The import saving is larger, at about $960,000 a year, so even after the price cut Ossett keeps roughly half the benefit, and lower shelf prices can lift volume and footfall in all 6 shops ahead of opening a 7th store [app]. Winning midlands shoppers now — before rivals respond — builds loyalty, and accessory sales typically follow tablet purchases, compounding the gain [an]. However, Option B holds prices and uses the saving to fund a 7th shop in the northern suburbs [k]. Retaining the full margin grows profit comfortably beyond last year's $410,000 and funds expansion without borrowing, the bigger long-term prize [app]. The danger is that rivals cut prices first, and Ossett, holding price, loses volume and carries excess tablet stock through the crucial winter season [an]. Overall, I think Ossett should choose Option A [eval], because the $480,000 cut is affordable from a $960,000 saving and the extra share and loyalty are what the northern expansion will live or die by; it should run the promotion for the autumn only, review sales weekly, and bank the surplus toward the 7th shop if the uplift is weak [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: 8% price cut costing $480,000 to drive volume and share
Option B: hold prices and use the saving to fund a 7th shop
application_max_2: $480,000 of the about $960,000 annual saving returned to shoppers
Reference to $6,000,000 tablet sales / $410,000 profit / 6 shops / 20,000 tablets
analysis_max_2: Chain from price cut to higher footfall and loyalty to compounding accessory sales
Chain from holding prices to banked margin but lost volume if rivals cut first
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Garrowby Grain Co is a partnership in Country X growing wheat and milling flour for export to Country W, while importing all its fertiliser and tractor parts from Country W. It exports 9,000 tonnes of flour a year at $420 a tonne, worth $3,780,000, and imports €700,000 of fertiliser. It also buys replacement tractors from a Country W dealer every few years. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro.

Partner Edward Garrowby must decide on next season's export pricing. Option A is to sign a two-year export deal at $420 a tonne, fixing dollar revenue. Option B is to quote Country W buyers in euros and let revenue move with the rate. The partnership employs 23 staff and farms 2,600 hectares.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a weaker currency on a business that both imports and exports.
questions.model_answer: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers, so export orders and sales may rise [1]. Imports become more expensive in local currency, so the cost of raw materials and parts rises [1].

knowledge_max_2: Exports become cheaper for foreign buyers / export demand may rise
Imports become more expensive in local currency / input costs rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Garrowby Grain Co.
questions.model_answer: First, its flour exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $420 a tonne, flour now costs buyers about €269 per tonne instead of €323, so the 9,000-tonne offer becomes more attractive against Country W domestic mills [app]. Second, imported inputs become more expensive for the partnership [k]. The €700,000 fertiliser and tractor parts bill rises from $910,000 to $1,092,000, an extra $182,000 a year [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers
A depreciation makes imports more expensive in local currency
application_max_2: Reference to €269 vs €323 per tonne at $420 a tonne / 9,000 tonnes of flour
Reference to the €700,000 fertiliser bill rising from $910,000 to $1,092,000

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to sign a two-year export deal at $420.
questions.model_answer: First, a two-year deal at $420 a tonne fixes dollar revenue [k]. With 9,000 tonnes a year, the partnership is guaranteed $3,780,000 in each of the two years, regardless of how the rate moves [app]. Predictable inflows make it far easier to plan cash for the higher fertiliser bills and tractor-part purchases, cutting the risk of short-term borrowing [an]. Second, it removes the risk of an unfavourable move in the exchange rate against the partnership [k]. If the dollar rebounds towards $1.30, euro-quoted revenue under Option B would shrink, but Option A pays out the agreed $420 per tonne in dollars [app]. Certainty also strengthens the partnership's case for credit with suppliers and its bank, easing investment across its 2,600 hectares [an].

knowledge_max_2: Fixing the price gives revenue certainty over two years
Fixing the price removes exposure to adverse exchange-rate moves
application_max_2: Reference to $420 x 9,000 tonnes = $3,780,000 a year guaranteed
Reference to $1.30 rebound scenario / 2,600 hectares / fertiliser bills
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed revenue to reliable cash planning to avoiding short-term borrowing
Chain from removed rate risk to stronger credit standing to easier investment

questions.question_text: Do you think Garrowby Grain Co should sign the two-year export deal at $420 (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A fixes export revenue at $420 a tonne — $3,780,000 a year for two years on 9,000 tonnes [k]. It guarantees cash far above the extra $182,000 fertiliser cost and lets management plan drilling, buying and 23 staff wages with confidence through 2027 and 2028 [app]. The trade-off is giving up the upside: if the dollar weakens further beyond $1.56, an euro-quoted deal would have paid more dollars, so signing now caps the benefit just when the currency is most favourable [an]. However, Option B quotes Country W buyers in euros and lets revenue float with the rate [k]. If the dollar stays weak or weakens further, euro-invoiced sales could bring in well over $3,780,000, but if it strengthens back towards $1.30, dollar revenue falls and margins compress exactly when input costs stay high [app]. The partnership would carry the full currency risk with no certainty, which is uncomfortable for a 23-staff business farming 2,600 hectares with thin cash cover [an]. Overall, I think Garrowby should choose Option A [eval], because certainty on $3,780,000 a year matters more to a partnership facing a certain $182,000 rise in import costs than speculative gains from further depreciation; it can revisit currency terms when the two-year deal expires [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: two-year deal fixes $420 per tonne ($3,780,000 a year)
Option B: euro-quoted pricing lets revenue float with the exchange rate
application_max_2: Reference to $3,780,000 annual revenue / 9,000 tonnes / $420 a tonne
Reference to $1.56 and $1.30 per euro / $182,000 extra fertiliser cost / 23 staff / 2,600 hectares
analysis_max_2: Chain from fixed deal to predictable cash to confident planning of wages and inputs
Chain from euro quoting to either gains above $3,780,000 or falling dollar revenue and squeezed margins
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and the extra fertiliser cost

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Amberfell Instruments is a private limited company in Country X building laser levels for construction firms in Country W. It exports 1,500 units a year at $380 each, worth $570,000. The dollar has swung between $1.25 and $1.60 per euro over the past year, so profit is hard to predict at budget time.

Director Lena Kovac must decide how to invoice 2027 orders. Option A is to invoice in Country X dollars at $380 a unit and shift the risk to buyers. Option B is to invoice in euros at €304 a unit, giving $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro. The firm employs 24 specialists, buys imported lenses costing €96,000 a year, and holds almost no dollar cash reserves, so swings bite within weeks.

questions.question_text: Calculate the dollar revenue at $1.25 and $1.60 per euro if 1,500 units are invoiced at €304 each.

knowledge_max_2: Correct calculation at $1.25 per euro: $570,000
Correct calculation at $1.60 per euro: $729,600

questions.question_text: Explain two problems the exchange-rate swing creates for Amberfell Instruments.
questions.model_answer: First, it makes annual revenue unpredictable [k]. Invoicing in euros could yield $570,000 at $1.25 per euro or $729,600 at $1.60 per euro — a difference of $159,600 on exactly the same sales of 1,500 units [app]. Second, the firm finds costing and pricing very difficult [k]. It cannot set firm budgets for wages for 24 specialists or for imported lenses when the payout for identical orders can swing by six figures in a single year [app].

knowledge_max_2: Exchange-rate swings make revenue unpredictable
Exchange-rate swings make budgeting and pricing decisions difficult
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 vs $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to the $159,600 swing / 1,500 units / 24 specialists

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option B, to invoice in euros at €304.
questions.model_answer: First, euro invoicing appeals strongly to Country W buyers [k]. A fixed €304 per unit removes currency risk for the construction firms, so their purchasing departments can approve orders without worrying about monthly rate moves [app]. Lower buyer risk should win repeat orders against rivals who quote in volatile currencies, keeping the workshop fuller [an]. Second, if the dollar weakens further, euro invoices convert to more dollars [k]. At $1.60, 1,500 units at €304 yield $729,600 — $159,600 above the $570,000 floor — while the imported lenses at €96,000 a year also cost more dollars at the same time [app]. This partial natural offset protects margin without any special financial instruments [an].

knowledge_max_2: Invoicing in the buyer's currency removes buyer risk and can win orders
A weaker dollar raises the local-currency value of foreign earnings
application_max_2: Reference to €304 fixed unit price appealing to Country W construction firms
Reference to $729,600 at $1.60 vs $570,000 at $1.25 and €96,000 lenses rising in dollar terms
analysis_max_2: Chain from buyer price certainty to more repeat orders and fuller capacity
Chain from euro invoicing to revenue and lens costs moving together to protected margin

questions.question_text: Do you think Amberfell Instruments should invoice 2027 orders in euros at €304 (Option B)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option B invoices in euros at €304 per unit, so Country W buyers face a stable price and no currency risk [k]. That should help Amberfell win and keep contracts in a market where buyers prefer simplicity, and at $1.60 the same invoices yield $729,600, comfortably covering the €96,000 lens cost and lifting margin well above the $570,000 floor [app]. The trade-off is that if the dollar strengthens towards $1.25, Amberfell receives only $570,000 from the same orders, with zero upside if the dollar weakens further [an]. However, Option A invoices in dollars at $380, fixing Amberfell's annual revenue at $570,000 whatever happens to the rate [k]. That gives complete certainty for budgeting 24 specialists' wages and removes the $159,600 swing, but it pushes all currency risk onto buyers: at $1.60 they would pay just €237.50, while at $1.25 they pay €304, which buyers will resist [app]. The risk is losing price-sensitive orders to suppliers who quote in euros [an]. Overall, I think Amberfell should choose Option B [eval], because revenue and lens costs are both priced in euros, so euro invoicing creates a natural balance that a dollar invoice cannot match; it should monitor the rate monthly and raise the €304 price if the dollar strengthens persistently [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option B: euro invoicing at €304 gives buyers price certainty
Option A: dollar invoicing at $380 fixes revenue but shifts risk onto buyers
application_max_2: Reference to $570,000 at $1.25 and $729,600 at $1.60 per euro
Reference to $380 dollar price / €96,000 lenses / 24 specialists / Country W buyers
analysis_max_2: Chain from euro invoicing to buyer certainty to more orders and natural offset of euro costs
Chain from dollar invoicing to fixed $570,000 but buyers resisting a swinging euro price
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes monitoring the rate monthly

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Larkhill Brewery Co is a private limited company in Country X brewing craft ale for pubs and bottle shops. It exports 30% of its 480,000 litres a year to Country W at $6 a litre — 144,000 litres worth $864,000 — and imports hops from Country W at €320,000 a year. The Country X dollar has depreciated from $1.30 per euro to $1.56 per euro.

Founder Sofia Almeida must decide the 2027 strategy. Option A is to expand exports, since the ale is now cheaper for Country W buyers at about €3.85 a litre instead of €4.62. Option B is to raise domestic pub prices by 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 to offset pricier hops. The brewery employs 14 staff and made $290,000 profit last year.

questions.question_text: State two effects of a depreciation on a business that imports its raw materials.
questions.model_answer: Imports become more expensive in the local currency, so raw material costs rise [1]. Profit margins are squeezed because prices cannot always be raised to cover the higher input costs [1].

knowledge_max_2: Imports become more expensive in local currency
Profit margins are squeezed / input costs rise

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the depreciation on Larkhill Brewery Co.
questions.model_answer: First, its ale exports become cheaper for Country W buyers [k]. At $6 a litre, the 144,000 litres exported now cost buyers about €3.85 a litre instead of €4.62, making the push into Country W more competitive without cutting the dollar price [app]. Second, imported hops become more expensive for the brewery [k]. The €320,000 hop bill rises from $416,000 to $499,200 a year, an extra $83,200 of cost [app].

knowledge_max_2: A depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers
A depreciation makes imported raw materials more expensive
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 per litre / 144,000 litres / $864,000 export revenue
Reference to the €320,000 hop bill rising from $416,000 to $499,200 (extra $83,200)

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of choosing Option A, to expand exports.
questions.model_answer: First, expanding exports exploits the weaker currency immediately [k]. With ale effectively cheaper at €3.85 a litre, Larkhill can pitch to new Country W pubs and bottle shops without cutting its $6 price [app]. Winning accounts now locks in demand before rivals adjust, spreading fixed brewhouse costs over more litres and lifting profit beyond the $290,000 of last year [an]. Second, growing beyond the 30% export share reduces reliance on Country X pubs [k]. Increasing output past the 144,000 litres now shipped abroad diversifies the customer base across two countries [app]. Diversification protects revenue if domestic pub closures or duty changes hurt the home market, and export success can later support stronger negotiating positions with distributors [an].

knowledge_max_2: A weaker currency lets the business expand exports without cutting price
Export growth reduces dependence on the domestic market / diversifies risk
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 a litre / $6 price / pitching to new Country W pubs
Reference to 30% export share / 144,000 litres / $290,000 profit last year
analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to locked-in demand to fuller capacity and higher profit
Chain from diversification to protected revenue if the home market weakens

questions.question_text: Do you think Larkhill Brewery Co should expand exports (Option A)? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Option A expands exports while ale is cheap for Country W buyers at about €3.85 a litre [k]. The existing 144,000 litres already earn $864,000, and each extra litre sold at $6 adds margin while the dollar stays weak, so expanding now is the highest-return use of the brewery's capacity [app]. Success would spread fixed costs further and could lift profit well above the $290,000 achieved last year [an]. However, Option B raises domestic pub prices by 4% on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640 [k]. That almost covers the $83,200 extra cost of imported hops, protecting margins with no overseas risk, no new working capital and no sales effort in a foreign market, and pubs usually accept modest rises more easily than large ones [app]. The danger is that 4% may still put some price-sensitive drinkers off, and it does nothing to capture the cheap-ale window or to cut dependence on the 70% domestic share [an]. Overall, I think Larkhill should choose Option A [eval], because the depreciation is temporary and only Option A converts it into lasting market position and profit growth; the brewery should keep domestic prices under review and apply Option B if export orders disappoint or the dollar rebounds [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Option A: expand exports while the ale is cheap for Country W buyers
Option B: 4% domestic price rise on $2,016,000 of sales, gaining $80,640
application_max_2: Reference to €3.85 vs €4.62 a litre / $6 price / $864,000 export revenue
Reference to $80,640 vs $83,200 extra hop cost / $290,000 profit / 144,000 litres / 70% domestic share
analysis_max_2: Chain from cheaper ale abroad to growing export volume to spread fixed costs and higher profit
Chain from 4% domestic rise to covered hop costs but lost share and untapped export opportunity
evaluation_max_2: Clear, justified recommendation between Option A and Option B
Weighs both options using stem figures and proposes keeping Option B under review
